reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Sporadic, almost always de novo dominant disorder caused by a recurrent LMNA variant that generates the toxic truncated lamin A protein progerin
Infants appear normal at birth but develop failure to thrive and characteristic features within the first one to two years
Distinctive appearance includes alopecia, prominent scalp veins, micrognathia, a beaked nose, prominent eyes and loss of subcutaneous fat
Skeletal changes include delayed dentition, coxa valga, a horse-riding stance and progressive joint contractures with distal resorption (acro-osteolysis)
Intelligence is preserved, distinguishing it from many other progeroid conditions
Progressive severe atherosclerosis leads to myocardial infarction and stroke, the principal causes of death
Skin becomes sclerodermatous and mottled with pigmentary change over the trunk
Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by molecular testing for the characteristic LMNA variant
reference.pathophysiology: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome is usually caused by a de novo point variant in LMNA that activates a cryptic splice site, producing progerin, a truncated lamin A that cannot be properly processed and remains farnesylated. Accumulation of progerin distorts the nuclear envelope, destabilises the nuclear lamina and disrupts chromatin organisation, DNA repair and mechanotransduction. This drives premature cellular senescence and, in vascular smooth muscle, accelerated atherosclerosis that dominates the clinical course.
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the recurrent LMNA variant
Echocardiography and vascular imaging for atherosclerotic and cardiac disease
Lipid profile and cardiovascular risk assessment
Skeletal survey for acro-osteolysis, coxa valga and joint contractures
Dental review for delayed and crowded dentition
redFlags: Chest pain, syncope or other features of myocardial ischaemia
Focal neurological signs suggesting transient ischaemic attack or stroke
Severe joint contractures compromising mobility and function
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive and life-limiting, with death typically in the second decade, most often from myocardial infarction or stroke secondary to accelerated atherosclerosis. Multidisciplinary supportive care and cardiovascular risk management are central, and disease-modifying therapy targeting protein farnesylation has been developed.
pitfalls: Confusing preserved intelligence with other progeroid syndromes that feature cognitive impairment
Underestimating cardiovascular risk in a young child and delaying cardiology involvement
Attributing early features to a non-syndromic failure to thrive
Overlooking the sclerodermatous skin as a diagnostic clue
management: Disease-modifying therapy with the farnesyltransferase inhibitor lonafarnib, which reduces progerin toxicity and improves survival
Cardiovascular risk reduction with antiplatelet therapy and a statin, and active management of ischaemic heart disease and cerebrovascular events driven by accelerated atherosclerosis
Nutritional support for failure to thrive with frequent high-energy feeds and dietetic input
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for joint contractures, with orthopaedic and podiatry care for coxa valga and other skeletal problems
Regular cardiology and vascular surveillance with echocardiography and vascular imaging, plus dental review for delayed and crowded dentition
Skin care, hydration and avoidance of trauma as part of general multidisciplinary supportive care
Genetic counselling for the family, noting most cases are sporadic de novo LMNA variants
